title: Welcome and Table of Contents
summary: What SS2 English Language Third Term is about and a map of every unit.

p: This term you revise all twelve tenses, study conditional and complex sentences, prefixes, active and passive voice, concord, adjuncts, conjuncts and disjuncts, sentence structures, prepositional phrases and idioms. In oral English you study stress and vowel contrasts. In writing you practise speeches, articles, expository essays and summaries of talks and of implied meaning. You also build vocabulary from publishing, industry, hotels and catering, and politics and government.
At the end of every unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

title: Grammar: Revision of Tenses
summary: The twelve English tenses by time and aspect, their forms, main uses and examples, with the difference between the present perfect and simple past.

p: Tense shows time (past, present, future) and aspect (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous). Together they give twelve tenses.

Simple present (base verb, add -s for he, she, it): habits ('She walks to school every day'), general truths ('Water boils at 100 degrees'), timetables ('The film starts at 9 PM'), stative verbs ('I believe you').

Present continuous (am, is, are + verb-ing): actions now ('I am studying'), temporary situations ('He is staying with his cousin'), definite plans ('We are travelling to Lagos tomorrow'), annoyance with 'always' ('You are always interrupting').

Present perfect (has, have + past participle): a past action with a present result ('I have lost my wallet'), life experience ('She has visited Ghana three times'), unfinished action ('He has lived in London for ten years'; 'She has worked here since 2020').
Present perfect continuous (has, have + been + verb-ing): stresses duration ('She has been painting the room all morning'); recent temporary action ('I have been running').
Simple past (verb + -ed, or irregular): a completed action at a definite time ('I finished my homework last night'); a series of actions ('I woke up, brushed my teeth and went to work').

Past continuous (was, were + verb-ing): an action in progress at a past moment ('At 8 PM yesterday I was watching a film'); an interrupted action ('I was sleeping when the phone rang'); two actions at once ('While I was cooking, he was cleaning').
Past perfect (had + past participle): the past before the past ('When we arrived, the film had already started').
Past perfect continuous (had been + verb-ing): duration before another past action ('He had been waiting for an hour before she arrived').
Simple future (will + base verb; shall with I and we in formal offers): predictions ('I think it will rain'), spontaneous decisions ('The phone is ringing. I will get it'), promises and offers.
Future continuous (will be + verb-ing): in progress at a future time ('This time next Friday I will be flying to Abuja'); polite questions ('Will you be using the car tonight?').
Future perfect (will have + past participle): completed before a future time ('By 2030 I will have graduated').

Two people look at an empty parking space. 'I sold it' (simple past: finished, and we may ask when). 'I have sold it' (present perfect: the result matters now, the car is gone). 'I was watching television when the lights went out' (interruption). 'She was late because she had missed her bus' (the missed bus came first).

activity: Correct: 'I have seen that film last year' (I saw that film last year). Fill in: she ___ (live) in that house since 2010 (has lived); while I ___ (read) my father came in (was reading); I think it ___ (rain) tomorrow (will rain); the patient ___ (die) before the doctor arrived (had died). Write 5 to 7 sentences about a memorable day using simple past, past continuous and past perfect.

title: Grammar: Conditional and Complex Sentences
summary: Types 0, 1, 2 and 3 of the conditional, the subjunctive 'were', and complex sentences with main and subordinate clauses.

p: A conditional sentence has an if-clause (the condition) and a main clause (the result).
Type 0 (general truths): if + simple present, simple present. 'If you heat ice, it melts.'
Type 1 (likely): if + simple present, will + base verb. 'If it rains tomorrow, the match will be cancelled.'

Type 2 (unlikely or imaginary, present or future): if + simple past, would + base verb. 'If I won the lottery, I would buy a private jet.' In careful English use 'were' for all subjects: 'If I were you, I would apologise.' (the subjunctive).
Type 3 (impossible, past; regret): if + past perfect, would have + past participle. 'If I had studied harder, I would have passed.' 'If she had taken the earlier train, she would not have been late.'

Type 1: 'If I have enough money, I will buy a car' (a real plan). Type 2: 'If I had enough money, I would buy a car' (a dream; I do not have it). Type 3: 'If I had had enough money, I would have bought a car' (a past regret). 'If he spoke French, he would get the job in Paris' is Type 2 (he does not speak French). 'If I see him, I will tell him' is a real possibility; 'If I saw him, I would tell him' is unlikely.

A complex sentence has one main (independent) clause and at least one subordinate (dependent) clause. A main clause can stand alone. A subordinate clause cannot; it often begins with if, when, because, although, who, which or that. 'The match will be cancelled [main] if it rains tomorrow [subordinate].' 'The student [who won the prize] was very happy.' 'Although it was raining [subordinate], we went for a walk [main].'

activity: Complete: (a) If you mix red and blue, you ___ purple (get); (b) If I ___ invisible for a day, I ___ to people's private conversations (were, would listen); (c) She ___ the exam if she ___ properly (would not have failed, had revised). Correct: 'If I was the president, I will reduce taxes' (If I were the president, I would reduce taxes). Main and subordinate clause in 'The book that I borrowed from the library is overdue': main: The book is overdue; subordinate: that I borrowed from the library.

title: Writing: Speech Writing
summary: The features and structure of a speech (title, salutation, introduction, body with rhetorical devices and conclusion), how it differs from an article, and a prize-giving day outline.

p: A speech is a formal address to an audience. It is written to be heard, not read, and that shapes its structure and language. It may inspire, persuade, inform or entertain.

Title: clear and striking ('The Peril of Plastic: A Call to Action'). Salutation: a formal greeting that respects the audience's ranks ('The Honourable Minister of Education, the Principal, members of the Board of Governors, dedicated staff, proud parents and my fellow students'). Introduction: a hook (a quotation, statistic, question or short story); the occasion; the thesis or central message. Body: two to four organised paragraphs using rhetorical devices: rhetorical questions ('How many of you wish to see a cleaner environment?'), repetition or anaphora ('We must act. We must lead. We must change.'), the rule of three ('honour, duty and legacy'), personal stories and direct address ('we', 'you', 'our'). Conclusion: sum up, end with a memorable statement, a call to action or hope, and thank the audience.
Study the table.

sections.h: Outline for a prize-giving day speech
p: Title: 'Celebrating Excellence, Inspiring Futures'. Salutation to the chairman, principal, teachers, parents, guests and fellow students. Introduction: a greeting and honour of the occasion; thesis: we honour achievers and reflect on the qualities that lead to success. Body 1: congratulate the winners ('diligence bears sweet fruit'). Body 2: encourage those without prizes ('let this ceremony be a catalyst, not a conclusion'). Body 3: thank teachers and parents. Conclusion: today's excellence is the foundation of tomorrow's success; thanks; a closing line.

activity: You are the Senior Prefect. Write a 250-word speech for Prize-Giving Day that welcomes the guests formally, congratulates winners sincerely, encourages other students and ends memorably.

title: Grammar: Affixation (Prefixes)
summary: What a morpheme and a prefix are, and the main negative, time, number and other prefixes with examples.

p: Affixation adds a morpheme (the smallest unit of meaning) to a root word to make a new word. A prefix goes at the beginning (un- + happy = unhappy); a suffix goes at the end (hope + -ful = hopeful). A prefix usually changes meaning but not word class. The choice of prefix often depends on the first letter of the root.
Study the table.

Add a negative prefix: responsible becomes irresponsible (r); legal becomes illegal (l). 'Unappear' is not a word; 'disappear' means to vanish. The prefix un- often reverses an action: lock, unlock; do, undo; wrap, unwrap; plug, unplug.

activity: Form opposites: accurate (inaccurate), comfortable (uncomfortable), respectful (disrespectful), understand (misunderstand), efficient (inefficient). Explain: international (between nations), reconstruct (build again), multilingual (many languages). Use re-, mis- and non- in three sentences.

title: Writing: Summarising a Talk or Lecture
summary: The three-step process (before, during and after the lecture), signpost language and shorthand.

p: You cannot re-read a speaker's words, so summarising a talk depends on active listening and efficient notes that separate main ideas from details at once.
Before: find out the topic if you can (background makes key terms easier), and have a notebook and pen; avoid distractions.

During: do not transcribe; capture ideas. Listen for signpost language: introducing the main idea ('My central argument is...', 'The key point is...'); listing ('There are three main reasons... First... Second... Finally...'); examples ('For instance...', 'To illustrate...'); emphasis ('It is crucial to remember...', 'Most importantly...'); concluding ('In conclusion...', 'To sum up...'). Use shorthand: & or + (and), w/ (with), w/o (without), an arrow (leads to), e.g., cf. (compare), govt, devt. Keep the skeleton (thesis and main supporting arguments); skip jokes, long stories and repetition.

After: review your notes at once while memory is fresh and fill gaps; find the core message (thesis); list two to four key points; write one paragraph in your own words combining them with no opinion; edit for brevity and clarity.

activity: Your teacher gives a 3 to 4-minute talk on 'The benefits of reading' or 'The importance of clean water'. Take notes and then write a one-paragraph summary of no more than 80 words with no opinion.

title: Grammar: Forming and Using the Passive Voice
summary: The four-step method for changing active to passive, a tense table, and four situations in which the passive is the better choice.

p: In the active voice the subject does the action ('The chef cooked the meal'): direct and strong. In the passive voice the subject receives the action ('The meal was cooked by the chef'): used when the doer is unknown, unimportant or when the action or receiver is to be stressed.

1. Find subject, verb and object: [The company] [built] [the house]. 2. Make the object the new subject: [The house]. 3. Change the verb to a form of 'to be' + the past participle, keeping the same tense: built becomes 'was built'. 4. Make the old subject the agent with 'by' (optional): 'The house was built by the company.'

p: When the doer is unknown ('My wallet was stolen'). When the doer is obvious or unimportant ('The suspect was arrested'; 'The new bridge will be opened next month'). To stress the action or receiver ('The Mona Lisa was painted by Leonardo da Vinci'). In scientific or formal writing ('The experiment was conducted under controlled conditions').

Change to active: the national anthem was sung by the students (The students sang the national anthem); the problem is being solved by the engineer (The engineer is solving the problem).

title: Oral English: the Dictionary and Spelling
summary: How to read a dictionary entry (spelling, pronunciation, word class, definitions, examples, derived forms and origin) and three spelling rules.

p: A dictionary tells you much more than spelling. Take 'profound': pro•found /prəˈfaʊnd/ adj. 1 very great or intense (profound despair). 2 showing great knowledge or insight (a profound philosopher). Derived form: profoundly. Origin: from Latin profundus 'deep'.

Spelling and word division (pro•found); pronunciation in the IPA (the stress mark shows stress on the second syllable); word class (adj. = adjective); numbered definitions, from most to least common; example phrases that show use; derived forms; and origin (etymology), which helps you remember the meaning.
'i' before 'e' except after 'c' when the sound is /iː/: believe, field, piece; receive, deceive, ceiling. Exceptions: weird, seize, height, foreign.
Drop a final silent 'e' before a suffix that begins with a vowel: make, making; use, usable. Keep the 'e' to keep a soft 'c' or 'g': change, changeable.

Double the final consonant of a one-syllable word ending in a single vowel plus one consonant before a vowel suffix: run, running; big, bigger. This also applies to longer words stressed on the last syllable: begin, beginning.

activity: Look up 'conduct' in a good dictionary: its word classes, the pronunciation of each, the first definition of each and one common phrase. Correct: accomodate (accommodate), embarass (embarrass), neccessary (necessary), proffessor (professor). Which is right: recieve or receive? (receive.)

title: Writing: Article Writing
summary: The structure of a compelling article (catchy headline, by-line, hooking introduction, developed body, closing) with Nigerian topics and a comparison with a formal letter.

p: An article is written for a wide audience in a newspaper, magazine, journal or online. It informs, explains, describes or persuades. Unlike a speech it is written to be read, and unlike a letter it has no named addressee.

1. Headline: catchy (alliteration, a play on words or a question) and informative: 'The Plastic Plague: Choking Our Oceans'. 2. By-line: the author's name below the title. 3. Introduction (the hook): a startling statistic, an anecdote, a rhetorical question or a direct statement; it introduces the topic and your angle. 4. Body: one main idea per paragraph, each opening with a topic sentence, backed by facts, examples, quotations or statistics, linked with connectives (furthermore, on the other hand, as a result). 5. Conclusion: sum up, offer a solution, recommendation or prediction, and end with a strong final sentence.

An article has no addresses, no salutation, no 'Yours faithfully'; the author's name appears in the by-line under the title. A formal letter has both addresses, a salutation, a complimentary close and a signature. An article can be formal or informal but is always engaging; a letter is strictly formal.

activity: Write a 250 to 300-word article for your school magazine on 'The importance of vocational skills in Nigeria's modern economy', 'The menace of examination malpractice' or 'Why every student should join a school club', with a title, by-line, hook, at least three points and a conclusion.

o: One main idea and a topic sentence

title: Midterm Test Guide
summary: What the Third Term midterm test covers and a short practice drawn from Weeks 1 to 4.

p: The test covers Weeks 1 to 4: tenses, conditional sentences, active and passive voice, prefixes, the dictionary and spelling, speech and article writing, summarising a talk, and the vocabulary of the weeks and registers (publishing, industry). Section A is objective (40 marks): choosing verb forms, naming conditional types, changing voice, choosing the nearest meaning and filling gaps. Section B is theory (60 marks): an article, a comprehension and summary, and grammar tasks including three conditional sentences and rewriting a paragraph in the passive.

Choose: 'She ___ in Lagos since 2010' (has lived). 'By the time we arrived, the film ___' (had started). 'If I had known, I would have helped' is Type (3). 'If you heat water to 100°C, it ___' (boils). Change to passive: 'The chef prepared the meal' (The meal was prepared by the chef). Nearest meaning: 'His ardour for the project was infectious' (passion). 'The behemoth corporation dominated the market' (giant). Gap: 'The charity helped ___ families' (indigent). 'She tried to ___ her fears, but her hands shook' (dissemble).

Rewrite in the passive where possible: 'The company launched the new product last week. They advertised it on television and social media. Many people have already bought it.' (The new product was launched by the company last week. It was advertised on television and social media. It has already been bought by many people.)

activity: Write one original sentence for each type of conditional (1, 2 and 3), then write an article on 'The role of the youth in curbing corruption'.
